name: Linkwarden
tagline: Open-source collaborative bookmark manager that archives everything you save

pricing.paid: Cloud: $3/month per user billed yearly (25% off) or $4/month billed monthly
pricing.trial: 14-day free trial of Cloud, cancel anytime
pricing.notes: Self-hosting is free — Linkwarden is fully open source (AGPL-3.0) with all features included. The Cloud plan has no free tier beyond the trial and supports up to 30,000 links per user (expandable via support).

pros: Every saved link is preserved as a screenshot, PDF, and readable copy — link rot can't touch your library
Fully open source (AGPL) with free self-hosting and feature parity with the paid cloud
Optional AI tagging, including support for local models, so auto-organization can stay private
Collaborative collections with permissions, plus public sharing via a link
Cheap cloud hosting at $3–4/month per user with a 14-day trial
Official iOS and Android apps (launched late 2025) with share-sheet saving and offline caching
cons: No free cloud tier — free means running your own server
Search is keyword/full-text only; no semantic search, summaries, or chat
Mobile apps are new and still catching up to the web experience
Built for collecting and preserving, not reading — no reader queue, text-to-speech, or reading progress
bestFor: Self-hosters, researchers, and teams who treat bookmarks as an archive — anyone who wants a permanent, searchable copy of every page they save.
verdict: The best open-source answer to link rot; pick it for preservation and ownership rather than reading comfort or AI-powered recall.
overview: Linkwarden is an open-source, self-hostable bookmark manager focused on preservation and collaboration. Every saved link is automatically archived as a screenshot, a PDF, and a readable text copy — and can be pushed to the Wayback Machine — so bookmarks keep working even after the original page changes or disappears. Links are organized into nested collections with tags, optional AI-generated tags (including via local models for privacy), highlights and annotations, and full-text search across archived content. Collections can be shared publicly or edited collaboratively with per-user permissions. The project is AGPL-3.0 licensed with all features available when self-hosting for free; the official Cloud service costs $3/month per user billed yearly (or $4 billed monthly) after a 14-day trial and supports up to 30,000 links per user. Browser extensions cover Chrome, Firefox, and Edge, a REST API enables integrations, and official iOS and Android apps arrived in late 2025 with share-sheet saving and offline caching.

faqs.a: Yes, if you self-host: Linkwarden is fully open source under AGPL-3.0, and a self-hosted instance includes every feature at no cost beyond your server. The managed Cloud service has no permanent free tier — it costs $3/month per user billed yearly ($4 billed monthly) after a 14-day free trial.

Yes, very actively. Linkwarden has grown into one of the most popular open-source bookmark managers, with a public GitHub repository (19k+ stars), frequent releases, and official iOS and Android apps launched in late 2025. Development is funded by the Cloud subscription, giving it a sustainable model that pure-donation projects often lack.

faqs.q: What is the best Linkwarden alternative?
faqs.a: Among self-hosted tools, Wallabag is the reading-focused counterpart and Karakeep (formerly Hoarder) adds AI-heavier organization. For hosted apps, Raindrop.io offers a generous free tier, and Marqly is a strong option if finding saves matters more than archiving them — it auto-tags with AI and supports semantic search by meaning, plus highlights and YouTube summaries, though it is not self-hostable.

Yes. Linkwarden shipped an official iOS app in late 2025 with collections, tags, search, share-sheet saving, and cached data for offline viewing; it works with both Linkwarden Cloud and self-hosted instances. The app is new and still gaining features, so the web app remains the most complete way to manage a large library.

faqs.q: Can I export my data from Linkwarden?
faqs.a: Yes. Linkwarden exports your links as standard bookmark HTML or JSON from settings, and archived page copies (screenshots and PDFs) can be downloaded. A documented REST API allows full programmatic export. If you self-host, everything already lives in your own database and file storage, so portability is total by design.
